scope: Structure only: concept titles, unit order and prerequisite intent. No third-party curriculum text is reproduced, and no restricted source is ingested.
description: A full-year introductory chemistry course: matter and measurement, the atom and its electronic structure, bonding and molecular shape, nomenclature, the mole and stoichiometry, reactions in solution, gases, thermochemistry, condensed phases, solutions, kinetics, equilibrium, acids and bases, thermodynamics, electrochemistry, nuclear chemistry and organic chemistry.

concepts.title: Pure Substances and Mixtures
concepts.summary: A pure substance has a fixed composition throughout, while a mixture contains two or more substances that keep their own identities and can be separated by physical means.

concepts.title: Elements and Compounds
concepts.summary: An element cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical means, whereas a compound contains two or more elements combined in a fixed whole-number ratio.

concepts.title: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Mixtures
concepts.summary: A homogeneous mixture is uniform at the molecular scale, so any sample has the same composition, while a heterogeneous mixture has regions that differ in composition.

concepts.title: Physical and Chemical Properties
concepts.summary: A physical property such as density or melting point is observed without changing the substance, while a chemical property describes a reaction the substance undergoes.

concepts.title: Intensive versus Extensive Properties
concepts.summary: An intensive property such as temperature or density does not depend on sample size, whereas an extensive property such as mass or volume does.

concepts.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
concepts.summary: A physical change alters only state or form, but a chemical change produces a new substance and is recognised by a colour change, gas, precipitate or heat release.

topics.topic: Measurement, Units, and the Nature of Science

concepts.title: SI Base and Derived Units
concepts.summary: The SI system fixes seven base units, and every other unit, such as the newton or the joule, is a product or quotient of those base units.

concepts.title: Accuracy and Precision
concepts.summary: Accuracy is agreement with the accepted value while precision is agreement among repeated measurements, so a set of readings can be precise and still biased.

concepts.title: Significant Figures in Calculations
concepts.summary: A result carries no more certainty than its least certain input, so multiplication keeps the smallest significant-figure count and addition keeps the smallest decimal place.

concepts.title: Dimensional Analysis
concepts.summary: Multiplying by a ratio equal to one converts units while cancelling the unwanted unit, which is why the answer arrives carrying the unit the question asked for.

concepts.title: Scientific Notation and Order of Magnitude
concepts.summary: Writing a value as a coefficient between one and ten times a power of ten fixes its size, and the exponent alone gives its order of magnitude.

concepts.title: Dalton's Atomic Postulates
concepts.summary: Dalton's model treats each element as identical indivisible atoms combined in fixed ratios, which explains the law of definite proportions but cannot account for isotopes.

concepts.title: Discovery of the Electron
concepts.summary: Thomson's cathode-ray experiments showed that atoms contain negative particles, and their charge-to-mass ratio was the same whatever gas filled the tube.

concepts.title: Rutherford's Nuclear Model
concepts.summary: Alpha particles that rebounded from gold foil forced the positive charge and nearly all the mass into a tiny nucleus, leaving the rest of the atom as empty space.

concepts.title: Protons, Neutrons and Electrons
concepts.summary: A proton carries +1 charge and a neutron carries none, each with a mass of about 1 u, while an electron carries -1 charge and about 1/1836 of that mass.

concepts.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
concepts.summary: The atomic number Z counts protons and fixes the element, while the mass number A counts protons plus neutrons for one particular nuclide.

concepts.title: Nuclide Notation
concepts.summary: Nuclide notation places A as a superscript and Z as a subscript before the element symbol, so a uranium-238 symbol with 92 means 92 protons and 146 neutrons.

concepts.title: Isotopes of an Element
concepts.summary: Isotopes of one element share the proton count but differ in neutron count, so they are chemically nearly identical and differ in mass.

concepts.title: Atomic Mass as a Weighted Average
concepts.summary: The atomic mass listed on the periodic table is the abundance-weighted average of the isotope masses, so it is close to but usually not equal to any single isotope.

concepts.title: Cations and Anions
concepts.summary: A cation forms when an atom loses electrons and an anion when it gains them, so the nucleus is unchanged while the charge and radius are not.

concepts.title: Predicting Monatomic Ion Charge
concepts.summary: Main-group metals lose their few valence electrons and nonmetals gain electrons until the octet is complete, so group 1 forms 1+ and group 17 forms 1-.

concepts.title: Polyatomic Ions
concepts.summary: A polyatomic ion is a covalently bonded group of atoms with a net charge, such as the sulfate ion, and it behaves as one unit in a formula.

topics.topic: Light, Energy, and the Quantum Model

concepts.title: Wave Properties and the Speed of Light
concepts.summary: Frequency times wavelength equals the speed of light, so a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency and a more energetic photon.

concepts.title: Photons and Quantized Energy
concepts.summary: Light exchanges energy in photons of energy h times its frequency, which is why dim light above the threshold ejects electrons and bright light below it does not.
prerequisites: Wave Properties and the Speed of Light

concepts.title: The Bohr Model and Line Spectra
concepts.summary: The Bohr model allows only certain orbits, so an electron emits a photon whose energy equals the gap between two levels and the spectrum shows discrete lines.

concepts.title: Orbitals and Quantum Numbers
concepts.summary: Three quantum numbers fix an orbital and a fourth fixes the electron spin, and the Pauli principle allows at most two electrons of opposite spin in one orbital.

concepts.title: Filling Order and Hund's Rule
concepts.summary: Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy, with 4s below 3d, and Hund's rule keeps electrons unpaired with parallel spins before any orbital is doubled.

concepts.title: Noble-Gas Shorthand and Valence Electrons
concepts.summary: Replacing the filled inner shells with a noble-gas symbol leaves the outer configuration visible, and those outer electrons are the valence electrons that determine bonding.

concepts.title: Effective Nuclear Charge
concepts.summary: Effective nuclear charge is the nuclear charge minus the screening of inner electrons, and it rises across a period because the screening hardly changes while Z increases.

concepts.title: Atomic Radius Across and Down
concepts.summary: Atomic radius falls from left to right across a period and rises down a group, because an added shell outweighs the greater nuclear charge.

concepts.title: Ionization Energy and Electron Affinity
concepts.summary: Ionization energy rises across a period and falls down a group, and its dips at groups 13 and 16 come from an unpaired p electron and a paired p electron respectively.

concepts.title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding
concepts.summary: Ionic bonding transfers electrons from a metal to a nonmetal, covalent bonding shares them between nonmetals, and metallic bonding delocalises them over a lattice of cations.

concepts.title: Electronegativity and Bond Polarity
concepts.summary: A bond is polar when the electronegativity difference is roughly 0.4 to 1.7 and largely ionic above that, with the shared electrons drawn towards the more electronegative atom.

concepts.title: Lattice Energy
concepts.summary: Lattice energy grows with the product of the ion charges and falls as the ions get larger, which is why magnesium oxide melts far above sodium chloride.

concepts.title: Drawing a Lewis Structure
concepts.summary: Count the valence electrons, join the atoms with single bonds, complete the outer octets, then place the remainder on the central atom and form multiple bonds if it is short of an octet.

concepts.title: Formal Charge and Resonance
concepts.summary: Formal charge is the valence-electron count minus the electrons assigned to an atom, and structures that differ only in electron placement are resonance forms of one hybrid.

concepts.title: Octet Exceptions
concepts.summary: Beryllium and boron compounds can be electron deficient, a species with an odd electron count such as nitric oxide has an unpaired electron, and third-period atoms may exceed eight electrons.

concepts.title: VSEPR Electron-Pair Geometry
concepts.summary: Electron pairs repel and spread as far apart as possible, giving linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral arrangements for two to six pairs.

concepts.title: Lone Pairs and Molecular Shape
concepts.summary: A lone pair occupies more angular space than a bond, so it compresses the bond angles and turns tetrahedral electron geometry into trigonal pyramidal or bent molecular shape.

concepts.title: Molecular Polarity from Dipole Cancellation
concepts.summary: A molecule is polar only when its bond dipoles do not cancel, so carbon dioxide is nonpolar even though each carbon-oxygen bond is polar.

concepts.title: Hybrid Orbitals and Valence Bond Theory
concepts.summary: Mixing s and p orbitals gives sp, sp2 or sp3 hybrids whose directions match the observed bond angles, which is how the tetrahedral carbon of methane is explained.

concepts.title: Sigma and Pi Bonds
concepts.summary: A sigma bond comes from head-on overlap and permits rotation, while a pi bond comes from side-on p overlap that holds the atoms in a plane and blocks rotation about a double bond.
prerequisites: Hybrid Orbitals and Valence Bond Theory

concepts.title: Molecular Orbital Theory
concepts.summary: Combining atomic orbitals gives bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals, and filling them in order explains why oxygen is paramagnetic although its Lewis structure shows no unpaired electrons.

concepts.title: Charge Balance in Ionic Formulas
concepts.summary: An ionic formula is written so the total positive charge equals the total negative charge, which is why aluminium oxide is Al2O3 rather than AlO.

concepts.title: Naming Ionic Compounds
concepts.summary: Name the cation first and the anion second with an -ide ending, and add a Roman numeral when the metal can take more than one stable charge.

concepts.title: Hydrates
concepts.summary: A hydrate holds a fixed number of water molecules per formula unit, written after a dot, and heating drives that water off as a measurable mass loss.

concepts.title: Greek Prefixes in Molecular Names
concepts.summary: Binary molecular compounds use prefixes from mono- to deca- to state each atom count, and the mono- on the first element is dropped.

concepts.title: Naming Acids
concepts.summary: An acid of the form HX is named hydro-X-ic acid, while an oxyacid takes the -ous ending when its anion ends in -ite and -ic when the anion ends in -ate.

concepts.title: Rules for Assigning Oxidation Numbers
concepts.summary: Oxygen is -2 in compounds except with fluorine, hydrogen is +1 when bonded to a nonmetal, and the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound sum to zero.

concepts.title: Oxidation and Reduction as Electron Transfer
concepts.summary: An atom is oxidised when its oxidation number rises and reduced when it falls, so the two changes always occur together in one reaction.

concepts.title: The Mole and Avogadro's Number
concepts.summary: One mole contains 6.022 x 10^23 entities, so the mole converts a count of particles into an amount that can be weighed.

concepts.title: Molar Mass
concepts.summary: Molar mass is the mass in grams of one mole of a substance and is numerically equal to its formula mass in unified atomic mass units.

concepts.title: Converting Between Mass, Moles and Particles
concepts.summary: Mass, moles and particle count convert into one another through molar mass and Avogadro's number, with each ratio chosen so the given unit cancels.

concepts.title: Percent Composition by Mass
concepts.summary: Percent composition is the mass of one element in a mole divided by the molar mass, so water is 11.2% hydrogen by mass although two of its three atoms are hydrogen.

concepts.title: Empirical Formula from Mole Ratios
concepts.summary: The empirical formula is the smallest whole-number atom ratio, found by converting masses to moles and dividing through by the smallest count.

concepts.title: Molecular Formula from the Empirical Formula
concepts.summary: The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, and the multiplier is the molar mass divided by the empirical formula mass.

concepts.title: Conservation of Atoms in a Reaction
concepts.summary: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides, because a reaction only rearranges atoms and never creates or destroys them.

concepts.title: Balancing by Inspection
concepts.summary: Balance one element at a time and leave hydrogen and oxygen until last, adjusting only coefficients because changing a subscript would change the substance.
prerequisites: Conservation of Atoms in a Reaction

concepts.title: Mole Ratios from Coefficients
concepts.summary: The coefficients of a balanced equation give the mole ratio between any two substances, and that ratio is the only bridge from one substance to another.

concepts.title: Limiting Reactant
concepts.summary: The limiting reactant is used up first and sets the maximum product, while the excess reactant is still present when the reaction stops.

concepts.title: Percent Yield
concepts.summary: Percent yield is the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield times 100, and a value above 100 signals an impure or wet product rather than a better reaction.

concepts.title: Precipitation Reactions
concepts.summary: Two soluble salts exchange ions and a product of low solubility leaves solution as a solid, which a solubility table predicts before the reaction is run.

concepts.title: Acid-Base Neutralization
concepts.summary: An acid and a base react to give water and a salt, with the hydrogen ion and the hydroxide ion combining in a one-to-one ratio.

concepts.title: Dissociation and Spectator Ions
concepts.summary: A strong electrolyte dissociates completely in water, and the ions that appear unchanged on both sides are spectators omitted from the net ionic equation.

concepts.title: Strong and Weak Electrolytes
concepts.summary: A strong electrolyte ionises essentially completely, a weak electrolyte only partly and a nonelectrolyte not at all, which conductivity reveals.

concepts.title: Electron Transfer in Redox Equations
concepts.summary: In a redox reaction the oxidation number of the oxidised element rises and that of the reduced element falls, and the electrons lost must equal the electrons gained.

concepts.title: Displacement and Combustion Reactions
concepts.summary: A single-displacement reaction has a more reactive element replace a less reactive one, and complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water.

concepts.title: Molarity
concepts.summary: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, and because a solution's volume changes with temperature, so does its molarity.

concepts.title: Dilution
concepts.summary: Dilution adds solvent without changing the moles of solute, so the product of molarity and volume is constant before and after.

concepts.title: Titration to the Equivalence Point
concepts.summary: A titration reaches its equivalence point when the moles of titrant equal the moles required by the balanced equation, which need not be the point of neutral pH.

concepts.title: Gas Pressure and Its Units
concepts.summary: Gas pressure is force per unit area on the walls of its container, and one atmosphere equals 760 mmHg, 101.325 kPa and 14.7 pounds per square inch.

concepts.title: Boyle's and Charles's Laws
concepts.summary: At fixed temperature the volume of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure, and at fixed pressure the volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.

concepts.title: Avogadro's Law and the Combined Gas Law
concepts.summary: At fixed temperature and pressure equal volumes of gases hold equal moles, and combining the three laws makes pressure times volume over temperature constant for a fixed amount.

concepts.title: The Ideal Gas Equation
concepts.summary: The equation PV = nRT with R equal to 0.08206 litre-atmosphere per mole kelvin relates pressure, volume, amount and absolute temperature for a gas treated as non-interacting point particles.

concepts.title: Molar Volume at Standard Conditions
concepts.summary: One mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and one atmosphere, and 22.7 litres at one bar, so a gas volume can be read as an amount.

concepts.title: Gas Density and Molar Mass
concepts.summary: Rearranging the ideal gas law gives density equal to pressure times molar mass over RT, so measuring density at known pressure and temperature yields a molar mass.

concepts.title: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
concepts.summary: Each gas in a mixture exerts the pressure it would exert alone, and the total pressure is the sum of those partial pressures.

concepts.title: Volume Ratios in Gas Reactions
concepts.summary: Because equal volumes hold equal moles at the same temperature and pressure, gaseous reactants and products combine in the volume ratio of their coefficients.

concepts.title: Postulates of the Kinetic-Molecular Model
concepts.summary: Gas particles move randomly with negligible volume and no attractions, and the pressure they exert comes from collisions with the container walls.

concepts.title: Temperature and Molecular Speed
concepts.summary: Average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature, so at one temperature all gases share the same average kinetic energy but have different root-mean-square speeds.

concepts.title: Effusion and Diffusion
concepts.summary: Graham's law states that the rate of effusion is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass, so a lighter gas escapes through a small hole faster.

concepts.title: Internal Energy and the First Law
concepts.summary: The internal energy of a system changes by the heat added to it plus the work done on it, so energy is conserved and only moves between system and surroundings.

concepts.title: Specific Heat Capacity
concepts.summary: Specific heat is the energy needed to raise one gram of a substance by one kelvin, and the value of 4.18 joules per gram kelvin for water makes it a slow-warming thermal reservoir.
prerequisites: Internal Energy and the First Law

concepts.title: Enthalpy Change at Constant Pressure
concepts.summary: Enthalpy change is the heat exchanged at constant pressure, and a negative value means the system released energy to the surroundings.

concepts.title: Calorimetry
concepts.summary: A calorimeter finds the heat transferred from a temperature change using q equals mass times specific heat times temperature change, and a bomb calorimeter does it at constant volume instead of constant pressure.

concepts.title: Hess's Law
concepts.summary: Because enthalpy is a state function, the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whatever route is taken, so it can be assembled from steps that are easier to measure.

concepts.title: Standard Enthalpies of Formation
concepts.summary: The standard enthalpy of reaction is the sum of the formation enthalpies of the products minus that of the reactants, with each element in its standard state assigned zero.

concepts.title: London Dispersion Forces
concepts.summary: Instantaneous dipoles attract every pair of molecules, and the force strengthens with polarisability, which is why the larger halogens boil at higher temperatures.

concepts.title: Dipole-Dipole Forces and Hydrogen Bonding
concepts.summary: A hydrogen bond is the strong attraction between a hydrogen bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on another of those atoms, and it explains the high boiling point of water.

concepts.title: Ion-Dipole Forces
concepts.summary: An ion attracts the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule, and these ion-dipole attractions are what pull sodium chloride apart in water.

concepts.title: Vapour Pressure and Boiling
concepts.summary: Vapour pressure rises with temperature, and a liquid boils when that pressure equals the external pressure, which is why water boils below 100 degrees Celsius on a mountain.

concepts.title: Energy Absorbed in Phase Changes
concepts.summary: Melting and vaporisation absorb energy without raising the temperature, so the heating curve of water has flat plateaus at 0 and 100 degrees Celsius.

concepts.title: Phase Diagrams and the Triple Point
concepts.summary: A phase diagram plots pressure against temperature, its triple point is where all three phases coexist, and its critical point ends the liquid-vapour boundary.

concepts.title: Crystalline and Amorphous Solids
concepts.summary: A crystalline solid has a repeating long-range lattice, while an amorphous solid such as glass lacks one and softens over a range instead of melting at a single temperature.

concepts.title: Classes of Crystalline Solids
concepts.summary: Molecular, ionic, covalent-network and metallic solids differ in what holds the lattice together, so a network solid such as diamond melts above 3500 degrees Celsius while molecular solids melt far lower.

concepts.title: Energetics of Dissolution
concepts.summary: A solute dissolves when the energy released by solute-solvent attractions offsets the energy needed to separate the solute particles and the solvent molecules.

concepts.title: Like Dissolves Like
concepts.summary: A polar solvent dissolves polar and ionic solutes while a nonpolar solvent dissolves nonpolar solutes, because the new attractions must resemble the ones they replace.

concepts.title: Molarity and Molality
concepts.summary: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so unlike molarity it does not change when the solution is heated or cooled.

concepts.title: Mass Percent and Parts per Million
concepts.summary: Mass percent compares solute mass with total solution mass, and parts per million scales the same ratio by 10^6 for trace concentrations.

concepts.title: Raoult's Law and Vapour Pressure Lowering
concepts.summary: A nonvolatile solute lowers the vapour pressure in proportion to its mole fraction, because solute particles occupy part of the surface otherwise available for evaporation.

concepts.title: Boiling Point Elevation and Freezing Point Depression
concepts.summary: Dissolved particles raise the boiling point and lower the freezing point by amounts proportional to molality, which is why salt melts ice on a road.
prerequisites: Raoult's Law and Vapour Pressure Lowering

concepts.title: Osmotic Pressure
concepts.summary: Osmosis moves solvent through a semipermeable membrane into the more concentrated solution, and the pressure that just stops it is proportional to molarity and absolute temperature.
prerequisites: Boiling Point Elevation and Freezing Point Depression

concepts.title: Expressing Reaction Rate
concepts.summary: Reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time, divided by the species coefficient so that one number describes the whole reaction.

concepts.title: Collision Theory and Activation Energy
concepts.summary: A reaction proceeds only when colliding molecules have at least the activation energy and the right orientation, so raising temperature raises the fraction of successful collisions.

concepts.title: Factors That Change Rate
concepts.summary: Concentration, surface area, temperature and catalysts change the rate by changing how often particles collide or how high the barrier is.

concepts.title: Rate Law and Reaction Order
concepts.summary: A rate law expresses rate as the rate constant times concentrations raised to experimentally determined powers, and those exponents sum to the overall order.

concepts.title: Determining Order from Initial Rates
concepts.summary: Order is found by comparing runs in which one concentration changes, because doubling a first-order reactant doubles the rate while doubling a second-order one quadruples it.

concepts.title: Half-Life of a First-Order Reaction
concepts.summary: A first-order reaction has a half-life equal to 0.693 divided by the rate constant, independent of starting concentration, which is why radioactive decay follows the same law.

concepts.title: Elementary Steps and the Rate-Determining Step
concepts.summary: A mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps that must sum to the balanced equation, and the slowest step controls the overall rate.

concepts.title: How a Catalyst Works
concepts.summary: A catalyst supplies a lower-energy pathway without being consumed, so it raises the rate in both directions and leaves the equilibrium constant unchanged.
prerequisites: Elementary Steps and the Rate-Determining Step

concepts.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
concepts.summary: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stop changing even though both reactions continue at the molecular level.

concepts.title: The Equilibrium Constant Expression
concepts.summary: The equilibrium constant is the product of product concentrations raised to their coefficients divided by the same expression for reactants, with pure solids and liquids omitted.

concepts.title: Interpreting the Magnitude of K
concepts.summary: A large K means products dominate at equilibrium and a small K means reactants dominate, but K says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.

concepts.title: The Reaction Quotient and Direction
concepts.summary: The reaction quotient has the form of K but uses current concentrations, so Q below K drives the reaction forward and Q above K drives it in reverse.

concepts.title: ICE Table Calculations
concepts.summary: An ICE table records initial and equilibrium concentrations with the change set by the stoichiometry, and K then supplies the equation that fixes the unknown.

concepts.title: Response to Concentration and Pressure Changes
concepts.summary: A system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change in concentration or partial pressure, and a catalyst does not shift it because it speeds both directions equally.

concepts.title: Temperature Dependence of K
concepts.summary: Changing the temperature changes the value of K itself rather than only the position, and an endothermic reaction is favoured by heating.
prerequisites: Response to Concentration and Pressure Changes

concepts.title: Bronsted-Lowry Proton Transfer
concepts.summary: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton and a base accepts one, so every acid has a conjugate base that differs from it by a single hydrogen ion.

concepts.title: pH and pOH
concepts.summary: pH is the negative base-ten logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, and at 25 degrees Celsius pH plus pOH equals 14 because the ion product of water is 1.0 x 10^-14.

concepts.title: Strong versus Weak Acids
concepts.summary: A strong acid ionises completely in water while a weak acid reaches an equilibrium, so solutions of equal concentration differ greatly in pH and conductivity.

concepts.title: Ka, Kb and the Conjugate Pair
concepts.summary: Ka measures the extent of weak-acid ionisation, and Ka times Kb equals the ion product of water for a conjugate pair, so a stronger acid has a weaker conjugate base.

concepts.title: Calculating the pH of a Weak Acid
concepts.summary: Solving the Ka expression for a weak acid gives the hydrogen ion concentration, and the shortcut that ignores the change in the denominator fails once the acid is not actually weak or dilute.
prerequisites: Ka, Kb and the Conjugate Pair

concepts.title: Percent Ionization
concepts.summary: Percent ionization is the fraction of acid molecules ionised times 100, and it falls as the initial concentration rises because the equilibrium shifts towards the intact acid.
prerequisites: Calculating the pH of a Weak Acid

concepts.title: Buffer Action
concepts.summary: A buffer resists pH change because it contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in comparable amounts, which neutralise any added acid or base.

concepts.title: The Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
concepts.summary: A buffer pH equals the acid pKa plus the logarithm of the conjugate base to acid ratio, and the buffer works best within about one pH unit of that pKa.

concepts.title: The Solubility Product Ksp
concepts.summary: The solubility product is the product of the ion concentrations in a saturated solution, each raised to its coefficient, and comparing Q with Ksp predicts whether a precipitate forms.

concepts.title: The Common Ion Effect
concepts.summary: Adding an ion that the salt already supplies lowers its solubility, because Q then exceeds Ksp and solid precipitates until Q returns to Ksp.

concepts.title: Entropy as Energy Dispersal
concepts.summary: Entropy measures how widely a system's energy is dispersed among microstates, so a process that spreads matter or energy over more arrangements has a positive entropy change.

concepts.title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.summary: A process is spontaneous when the total entropy of system plus surroundings increases, so an entropy decrease in the system is allowed if the surroundings gain more.

concepts.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity
concepts.summary: The free energy change equals enthalpy change minus temperature times entropy change, and at constant temperature and pressure a negative value means spontaneous while zero means equilibrium.

concepts.title: Temperature and Reaction Feasibility
concepts.summary: The signs of the enthalpy and entropy changes decide whether a reaction is always, never or only at some temperatures feasible, with the crossover at temperature equal to enthalpy change over entropy change.

concepts.title: Standard Free Energy and the Equilibrium Constant
concepts.summary: The standard free energy change equals minus RT times the natural logarithm of K, so a large negative value corresponds to a large equilibrium constant.

concepts.title: Splitting a Redox Reaction into Half-Reactions
concepts.summary: A redox reaction separates into an oxidation half-reaction and a reduction half-reaction, each balanced for atoms and charge before they are combined.

concepts.title: Balancing Redox in Acid and Base
concepts.summary: Balancing in acidic solution adds water and hydrogen ions to equalise atoms and charge, and in basic solution the same steps are followed before hydrogen ions are replaced by hydroxide.
prerequisites: Splitting a Redox Reaction into Half-Reactions

concepts.title: Galvanic Cells and the Salt Bridge
concepts.summary: In a galvanic cell oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, electrons flow through the external circuit and ions carry charge through the salt bridge.

concepts.title: Cell Notation and Electrolytic Cells
concepts.summary: Cell notation places the anode on the left and the cathode on the right, and an electrolytic cell uses an external supply to drive the reverse, nonspontaneous reaction.
prerequisites: Galvanic Cells and the Salt Bridge

concepts.title: Standard Reduction Potentials
concepts.summary: A cell potential is the cathode reduction potential minus the anode reduction potential, and a positive value means the cell reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

concepts.title: The Nernst Equation
concepts.summary: Cell potential falls as the reaction quotient rises, following the Nernst equation, which at 25 degrees Celsius reduces to the standard potential minus 0.0592 over n times the logarithm of Q.

concepts.title: Nuclear Stability and Binding Energy
concepts.summary: A nucleus is stable when the strong force outweighs proton repulsion, which is why the neutron-to-proton ratio needed for stability rises with atomic number and heavy nuclei decay.

concepts.title: Alpha, Beta and Gamma Decay
concepts.summary: Alpha decay lowers the mass number by four and the atomic number by two, beta-minus decay raises the atomic number by one, and gamma emission changes neither.

concepts.title: Half-Life of a Radionuclide
concepts.summary: After n half-lives the fraction of a radionuclide remaining is one half raised to n, so activity falls by half in every equal time interval.

concepts.title: Fission and Fusion Energy
concepts.summary: Fission splits a heavy nucleus and fusion joins light ones, and both release energy because the products are more tightly bound than the reactants.

concepts.title: Alkanes and Structural Isomerism
concepts.summary: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the formula CnH2n+2, and from butane onward the same formula admits branched isomers with different boiling points.

concepts.title: Alkenes, Alkynes and Aromatic Rings
concepts.summary: A carbon-carbon double or triple bond makes a hydrocarbon unsaturated, while the delocalised six-electron ring of benzene makes it aromatic.

concepts.title: Functional Group Families
concepts.summary: A functional group is the reactive part of a molecule, and its identity defines the family: hydroxyl for alcohols, carbonyl for ketones and aldehydes, carboxyl for acids.

concepts.title: Naming and Isomer Classes
concepts.summary: An organic name takes the longest carbon chain as parent and adds suffixes for the principal functional group, while constitutional isomers differ in connectivity and stereoisomers differ only in spatial arrangement.

concepts.title: Substitution, Addition and Elimination
concepts.summary: Alkanes react mainly by substitution, alkenes by addition across the double bond, and alkyl halides by elimination to form an alkene.

concepts.title: Addition and Condensation Polymers
concepts.summary: An addition polymer links monomers through their double bonds, while a condensation polymer forms by losing a small molecule such as water at each new link.
